candidates.description: The original study's findings that uses-and-gratifications dimensions predict newspaper readership patterns for weekday and Sunday subscribers, single-copy readers, and non-readers
candidates.citation_sentence: Note that if all seven hypotheses are accepted, the Towers study would have been replicated exactly.
candidates.notes: H2-H7 tested specific readership predictions; the discriminant analyses provided limited support for some but not all hypotheses (H2 strongly supported, H3 and H4 disappeared, H5 not supported, H6 supported, H7 partially supported), making the overall result inconclusive. candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that newspaper uses-and-gratifications statements formed three distinct dimensions: surveillance, diversion, and interaction; the replication tested this factor structure in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: The replication found two groupings, information and entertainment, rather than the original three-factor solution; the authors state that Hypothesis 1 could not be accepted. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that weekday newspaper subscribers were strongly oriented toward using newspapers to obtain immediate knowledge of big news events; the replication tested this relationship in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: The replication authors state that Hypothesis 2 was so strongly supported that the predicted relationships for weekday single-copy readers and non-readers disappeared. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that weekday single-copy readers were strongly oriented toward finding interesting or unusual stories to tell others; the replication tested this relationship in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: The predicted single-copy-reader relationship did not emerge in the replication. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that weekday newspaper non-readers were strongly oriented toward using a newspaper simply to pass the time; the replication tested this relationship in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: The replication authors state that the weekday non-reader relationship disappeared. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that Sunday newspaper subscribers were strongly oriented toward obtaining immediate knowledge of big news events, being happy, and getting more information about things they had seen; the replication tested these relationships in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: Only the immediate-knowledge relationship was supported; the predicted happiness and additional-information relationships disappeared, so the combined claim received partial support. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that Sunday single-copy readers were strongly oriented toward understanding what was going on and toward using the newspaper simply to pass the time; the replication tested these relationships in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: The paper's summary contains apparent hypothesis-numbering errors, but its results state that Sunday single-copy readers were not distinctively predicted and instead resembled subscribers in their orientation toward immediate knowledge. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications
candidates.description: The original study claimed that Sunday newspaper non-readers were strongly oriented toward using the newspaper to pass the time and to obtain more information about things they had seen; the replication tested these relationships in Sample II.
candidates.citation_sentence: Wayne M. Towers, "Weekday and Sunday Readership Seen Through Uses and Gratifications," Newspaper Research Journal 6:20-32 (1985).
candidates.notes: The replication found the predicted time-filler and event-information orientations, and the authors describe this result as clearly supporting the relevant hypothesis. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]
